tier_reason: The README states verbatim that BC7E is 'usually around 2-3x faster vs. ispc_texcomp at the same average quality (as measured by PSNR or SSIM), and up to ~8x faster vs. ispc_texcomp's "slow" profile', but gives no table, image set, hardware, ispc_texcomp version or harness; the repo holds only the encoder and an example packer (bc7enc.cpp), no comparison benchmark. First-party numbers without methodology, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: README build line: ispc -g -O2 bc7e.ispc --target=sse2,sse4,avx,avx2 --opt=fast-math --opt=disable-assertions; tested mostly with ispc 'v1.82' (as written, probably 1.8.2) and less with the bundled v1.10.0; example built with Visual Studio 2019. No compiler, flags, threading or machine are given for the speed claim itself.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 182 stars, 19 forks; the latest bc7e.ispc ships in richgel999/bc7enc_rdo (which todds uses for BC7), and bc7e.ispc was ported to plain C++ in basis_universal (encoder/basisu_bc7e_scalar.cpp)
corrections.caveats: Claims only: no benchmark table, hardware, image set, ispc_texcomp version or harness. The same 2-3x claim for Basis BC7 appears in the bc7enc README, so the evidence is first-party only. The 'slow' profiles are 'calibrated to compete against' ispc_texcomp's similarly named profiles, but matched-quality data is not shown. Both encoders encode blocks single-threaded per call (threading is the caller's job). The repo was archived on 2026-01-28; the README calls it an archive of the original release and says the latest bc7e.ispc (determinism fixes, better solid-colour blocks) is in richgel999/bc7enc_rdo, and points to the newer, faster bc7f. The repo ships a prebuilt ispc.exe. An independent comparison exists in Aras Pranckevicius's 'Texture Compression in 2020' blog post (2018 MacBook Pro, Core i9 2.9 GHz, Xcode 11.7, Mpix/s vs Luma-PSNR charts), but the blog is blocked here and the search snippet is directional only ('bc7e presets have either better quality or faster compression than ISPC').

notes: Baseline ispc_texcomp (Intel ISPCTextureCompressor) is the recognisable CPU BC7 incumbent; baseline_in_list false is correct because the category lists image codecs, not texture encoders. Archived means maintenance stays 'abandoned' even though the last commit (README edit) is 2026-01-28. Aras's independent blog numbers could support tier B if an environment reaches aras-p.info.

tier_reason: The README carries a first-party BC7 table (31 images, encode time and average PSNR) against ispc_texcomp and DirectXTex on an unnamed dual Xeon with OpenMP, no compiler or flags, and the comparison harness is not in the repo; the BC1 claims against libsquish and Compressonator have no numbers at all. First-party with partial methodology, and the 263x DirectXTex figure exceeds 50x with flags unstated, so C.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 243 stars, 24 forks; archived 2026-01-28; superseded by richgel999/bc7enc_rdo, which carries rgbcx and the bc7enc BC7 encoder
corrections.claimed_speedup: BC1: the README claims rgbcx's 'prioritized cluster fit' is 3-4x faster than traditional cluster fit (libsquish with SSE2) at the same or slightly higher average quality, and faster than AMD Compressonator and libsquish at the same average quality; no BC1 timings are given. BC7 (31 images, kodim plus others, multithreaded, encode time only), perceptual mode scored on REC709 luma PSNR: ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s 48.6 dB vs bc7enc16 uber0/max_partitions 64 38.3 s 49.6 dB (9.3x faster, derived from page data); ispc_texcomp fast 41.5 s 48.0 dB vs bc7enc16 uber0/16 20.8 s 49.3 dB (2.0x faster, derived from page data). Non-perceptual (RGB PSNR): ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s 46.8 dB vs bc7enc16 uber4/64 51 s 46.1 dB (7.0x faster at 0.7 dB lower, derived from page data); the later update at matched RGB PSNR shows parity: ispc_texcomp fast 41.45 s 46.09 dB vs latest bc7enc16 uber4/64 41.42 s 46.03 dB, or 38.78 s 45.94 dB with filterbank optimizations (1.07x, derived from page data); ultrafast: ispc_texcomp 1.9 s vs bc7enc16 3.8 s at 42.7 dB (ispc_texcomp 2x faster). DirectXTex CPU (locally patched) default 9485.1 s 45.6 dB vs bc7enc16 uber1/64 36 s 46.0 dB (263x faster, derived from page data); DirectXTex mode-6-only 466.4 s 41.9 dB vs bc7enc16 6.7 s 42.8 dB (70x faster, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Most timings are for the original bc7enc16 release (the README says the latest bc7enc16.c is 8-27% faster with mode 1 enabled); this repo's bc7enc.c adds alpha modes and is not exactly the code timed. The encoders do different work: bc7enc16 uses only BC7 modes 1 and 6 for opaque blocks while ispc_texcomp searches all modes, and the perceptual rows are scored on luma PSNR, the metric bc7enc16's perceptual mode optimizes and ispc_texcomp does not, which favours bc7enc16. At matched RGB PSNR the later update shows parity with ispc_texcomp fast, and in the ultrafast rows ispc_texcomp is faster (1.9 s vs 3.8 s at 42.7 dB non-perceptual; 1.9 s vs 8.9 s perceptual, where bc7enc16 scores 48.4 vs 46.2 dB). The test machine is an unnamed dual Xeon; compiler and flags are unstated; ispc_texcomp was called 64 blocks at a time with AVX; the comparison harness is not in the repo. The DirectXTex run used a locally patched pbit bugfix, and the page's own times (9485.1 s vs 355.4 s for ispc_texcomp slow) show DirectXTex's CPU BC7 path is a very slow baseline, so the 263x figure overstates the practical gain. The BC1 claims have no numbers on the page. The repo was archived on 2026-01-28, and its README calls the BC7 encoder unvectorized work in progress and points to bc7enc_rdo and bc7e.ispc. Dual-licensed MIT or Unlicense (public-domain option, no patent grant).

notes: All quoted numbers match the README rows; the corrected claim adds the matched-RGB-PSNR parity row and the DirectXTex mode-6 row so the headline wins are not read in isolation. Baselines ispc_texcomp, DirectXTex, libsquish and Compressonator are all recognisable texture-encoder incumbents; baseline_in_list false is correct. bc7enc_rdo (not in the list) is the maintained successor of both this repo and bc7e; the orchestrator may want to treat the three together.

tier_reason: The README's 'Performance (v0.9.2)' table times ECT -1 to -9 against gzip -9 and zopfli -i1/-i5/-i15/-i30 on enwik8 compressed to gzip format, stating macOS 12.5, Intel i7-7700HQ and clang but no compiler version, flags or command lines, and no benchmark script is in the repo. A single first-party run, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On enwik8 (100,000,000 bytes) compressed to gzip format, ECT v0.9.2: ECT -3 35,014,543 bytes in 16.2 s vs zopfli -i15 34,966,078 bytes in 3m 59.9s (14.8x faster at 0.14% larger, derived from page data); ECT -2 35,019,440 bytes in 14.8 s vs zopfli -i5 34,983,757 bytes in 2m 12.0s (8.9x faster at 0.10% larger, derived from page data); ECT -5 34,942,796 bytes in 25.1 s vs zopfli -i30 34,961,453 bytes in 6m 30.6s (smaller and 15.6x faster, derived from page data); ECT -9 34,937,781 bytes in 3m 17.9s vs zopfli -i30 (smaller and 2.0x faster, derived from page data); ECT -1 36,493,257 bytes in 3.5 s vs gzip -9 36,475,811 bytes in 5.8 s (1.66x faster at 0.05% larger, derived from page data). The repo publishes no PNG or JPEG numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang on macOS 12.5 (version and flags not stated); command lines not given. ECT defaults to single-threaded deflate (--mt-deflate is opt-in in src/main.cpp), so the ECT runs were probably single-threaded like zopfli, but the README does not say.
corrections.caveats: The only published benchmark is deflate (gzip) output on enwik8 text; there are no PNG or JPEG timings in the repo, so the record's numbers support general lossless compression (ECT gzip vs zopfli and gzip -9), not image codecs. ECT's deflate is built on a modified zopfli, so zopfli is the apt incumbent for maximum-compression deflate. Single run, old version (v0.9.2), no benchmark script, flags or command lines. ECT bundles modified copies of zopfli/zopflipng, mozjpeg, zlib, libpng, optipng, pngcrush, brotli, lodepng and Leanify under their own permissive licenses. An independent PNG optimizer benchmark that includes ECT exists at css-ig.net (benchmark/png-lossless), but it is blocked here and was not used.

notes: Category: the record's numbers compare ECT gzip vs zopfli and gzip -9, not ECT PNG optimisation vs OptiPNG/zopflipng, so file it under general-lossless (id kept unchanged). The rows were checked against the README table and the ratios recomputed; ECT -5 is added as the clearest smaller-and-faster comparison against zopfli -i30. A PNG-category entry would need the css-ig.net benchmark or similar from an environment that can reach it.
